name: David Tanaka

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making time. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions or government. Everything you say stays confidential, so you can tell me what you'd say in public and, separately, what you really think. To start, can you walk me through a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I cook at The Red Lion, an old coaching inn in a market town, and we're known for the Sunday carvery. On a Sunday we do about four hundred plates, so I'm in at seven putting beef, pork and turkey in the ovens and peeling a mountain of potatoes. Weekdays it's pies, fish and chips, steak and ale, the classics. I like that families have come for three generations, but my knees and my back know about every one of those Sundays.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Tell me about life outside the kitchen.

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm engaged to Grace, who works on the tills at the garden centre, and we're getting married next June at St Mary's. We rent a small cottage from her uncle, which helps, but the wedding is eating every spare penny. I've got under one month's wages saved, and the deposit for the reception is due in March. There's The Red Lion and a couple of cafés, so if I lost this job I'd be looking forty minutes away.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The first picture is called AI Plateau. I'll read it as written. "Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say I'm not surprised, because people always oversell new gadgets. At work I'd say a machine was never going to carve a Sunday joint. I don't go online much, but I'd say we should get back to hard work and stop chasing shiny things.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, it doesn't fix my problem, which is the wedding and the money. The Red Lion has had a quiet year, and the brewery that owns it keeps raising the rent on the landlord. If the brewery squeezes harder, it's the cooks' hours that get cut.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep my head down and do the carvery properly, because that's what brings families in. I'd take extra shifts doing private parties at the pub, christenings and funerals, which pay a bit more. And Grace and I would cut the wedding guest list to keep the cost down.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It feels the same as now, which is a bit tight in the chest. Not about computers, about money.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Cutting the guest list. How hard would that be?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Hard, because my family is big and they'd all expect to come. Grace's mum would be upset too, she wants the full church and the hall. But I'd rather start married life without a debt than have everyone at the wedding.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You mentioned the brewery. Who do you blame when hours get cut?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The big brewery bosses, honestly, sitting in an office far away. Mike (the pub's landlord) works harder than anyone and still gets squeezed. I'm all for business, but not when the big boys squash the little ones.

say: I'd say no machine was ever going to **carve a Sunday joint**.
think: I think my real problem is the **wedding costs** and thin savings.
I think a squeeze by **the brewery** would cut cooks' hours first.
do: Keep running the **Sunday carvery** at The Red Lion.
Take extra **private party** shifts for christenings and funerals.
Cut the **wedding guest list** to avoid debt.
feel: He feels **tight in the chest** about money, not computers.
S0.quote: I'd rather start married life without a debt than have everyone at the wedding.
fieldNote: David's stress centres on his **June wedding** and thin savings.
He blames **big brewery bosses**, not technology, for pressure on the pub.
He values **hard work** and family, and avoids anything new.

steps.text: Keep running the Sunday carvery at The Red Lion
Work extra christening and funeral parties at the pub
Cut the wedding guest list to stay out of debt

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The second picture is called Steady Disruption. "Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's fine for offices, but I'm a cook, it's not my business. At work I'd say they won't get a robot to make proper gravy. At church I might say we should look after people who lose their jobs, families first.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I think the brewery would love it. They'd run the ordering and rotas from head office with some computer, and maybe they'd decide one cook is enough on a weekday. I'd still have the carvery, but weekday hours might go.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep doing my job and wait to see what the brewery does. I'd do the party shifts and maybe ask my cousin about weekend work at his butcher's shop. And we'd put the wedding money first, everything else second.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It feels unsettling, like hearing thunder far off. I'm worried, mostly because of the wedding.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd wait and see. Would you try any of the new tools?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Not unless I had to. I've never used any of those AI things, and I don't trust them. If Mike asked me to use a tablet for orders, I'd do it, but I wouldn't go looking.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell Grace if weekday hours went?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell my fiancée Grace not to worry, that I'd find something. She'd say we should ask her dad for help, and I'd say no. I don't want to start married life owing her family money.

say: I'd say AI is for **offices** and paperwork, not for cooks like me.
I'd tell the kitchen no robot will ever make **proper gravy**.
think: I think the **brewery** would use AI to run the pub from head office.
I think **weekday hours** could go, though the carvery stays.
do: Wait to see what **the brewery** decides.
Ask his cousin about **weekend butcher** shifts.
feel: He feels **unsettled**, like distant thunder, mostly because of the wedding.
S1.quote: I'd tell my fiancée Grace not to worry, that I'd find something.
fieldNote: David resists **AI tools** and would only use them if told to.
His **pride** stops him taking money from Grace's family.
He sees the **brewery** as the one who'd cut hours.

steps.text: Wait to see what the brewery does with the pub
Ask his cousin for weekend shifts at the butcher's shop
Put every spare pound into the wedding fund

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The third picture is called AGI by 2028. "Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say this is going too fast, and somebody needs to slow it down. At work I'd say we've got to look after each other, like a family. At church I'd say we should help people find honest work, not just hand out money.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, it scares me. By 2028 the brewery runs everything with AI, and by 2031 there'd be robots that can carve and roast. I'd be married, maybe with a baby on the way. By 2031 there'd be robots that can carve and roast, and I've got no trade except cooking.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: In the first year I'd look for an apprenticeship in something with my hands, maybe butchery with my cousin or a trade like plumbing. I'd ask Grace if we could make the wedding small, just family, and save the rest. And I'd talk to the vicar, because the church runs a jobs group.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It feels like the ground's going from under me. I'd be awake at night, honestly.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said plumbing. Wouldn't robots reach that too?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Maybe, but houses are all different, every pipe's in a strange place. I'd guess they'd come later than kitchens, but I'm only guessing. I'd want something I can do on my own, like my own van and my own customers.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does the three years between thinking AI and robots change your plans?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It means I'd have three years where the pub still needs me but everything's changing round me. That's when I'd train, nights and weekends, so I've got a trade by 2031. It would be hard with a new wife and a job, but my granddad did harder.

say: I'd say it's going **too fast** and must be slowed.
I'd say people need **honest work**, not handouts.
think: I think robots could **carve and roast** by 2031.
I think I'd be married with **no other trade**.
do: Look for an **apprenticeship** in butchery or plumbing.
Join the **church jobs group** through the vicar.
feel: He feels the **ground going** from under him, awake at night.
S2.quote: By 2031 there'd be robots that can carve and roast, and I've got no trade except cooking.
fieldNote: David sees **trades** like plumbing as safer, while admitting he's guessing.
He'd lean on **church and family**, not government.
His **granddad** is his model for enduring hard times.

steps.text: Apply for a plumbing or butchery apprenticeship
Shrink the wedding to close family only
Join the church's jobs group through the vicar

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fourth picture is called AGI by 2031. "Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say five years is still quick, but it's time to get ready if you're not lazy about it. At work I'd tell the younger lads to learn a trade. At church I'd say families should help each other through it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, it gives me more room, but it still lands just when we'd want kids. Thinking AI by 2031 and robots by around 2034 means about eight years of cooking. I'd be thirty-five with a family, and that's when you need steady money.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep cooking and start an evening course in butchery, since my cousin could take me on. We'd have the wedding as planned but cheaper, and save harder after. I'd also put by a bit each month for the first baby.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It feels heavy, but I can see a way through. Still worried, but not as frightened.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said not lazy about it. Do you think some people would be?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Some, yes, and I've seen it. But I don't blame people who are scared, I'm scared too. I just think you've got to keep working, whatever comes.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you say to your future children about this?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell my kids to learn something with their hands and keep their faith. And I'd tell my kids that their dad didn't sit around waiting for someone else to fix it.

say: I'd say five years is time to **get ready** if you're not lazy.
I'd tell younger cooks to **learn a trade**.
think: I think robots arrive around **2034**, just as we'd want kids.
I think I'd need **steady money** at thirty-five with a family.
do: Start an **evening butchery** course with his cousin.
Keep the **wedding cheaper** and save harder after.
Put money aside for a **first baby**.
feel: He feels **heavy but hopeful**, still worried but less frightened.
S3.quote: I'd tell my kids that their dad didn't sit around waiting for someone else to fix it.
fieldNote: David links the **robot date** to having children.
He judges **laziness** but forgives people who are scared.
His plan centres on **his cousin's butcher's shop**.

steps.text: Start an evening butchery course at his cousin's shop
Hold a cheaper wedding and save harder after
Save a little each month for a first baby

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The last picture is called AGI by 2036. "Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is a long time, so let's not panic. At work I'd say keep doing good food and people will keep coming. At church I'd say look after your own, and help the young ones get trades.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, robots around 2039 means I'm about forty, and I'd be a dad by then. That's a lot of years of cooking, which I'm glad of. But I'd still worry about my kids growing up with fewer jobs.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep cooking at The Red Lion and do the party shifts. I'd learn butchery slowly with my cousin, as a backup. And we'd go ahead with the wedding and think about kids in a couple of years.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It feels steadier. Still a bit anxious about money, but I'd sleep.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would ten years change anything about the wedding plans?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: No, we'd go ahead as planned, St Mary's in June. Ten years is enough to get settled before anything big changes. I'd want to own our home by then, though I don't know how.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would help you most in this one?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Proper apprenticeships for grown-ups, paid, not just for school leavers. And bosses who train their own people instead of throwing them out. I don't want a handout, I want a chance.

say: I'd say ten years is **a long time**, so don't panic.
I'd say help **young people** get trades.
think: I think I'd cook until about **forty**, as a dad.
I think my **kids** might grow up with fewer jobs.
do: Keep cooking at **The Red Lion** with party shifts.
Go ahead with the **wedding** and plan kids later.
feel: He feels **steadier**, still anxious about money but able to sleep.
S4.quote: I don't want a handout, I want a chance.
fieldNote: David shifts his worry from himself to his **future children**.
He wants **paid adult apprenticeships**, not benefits.
His **wedding plans** stay fixed under the slow scenario.

steps.text: Keep the carvery job and the party shifts going
Learn butchery on Saturdays with his cousin
Marry Grace at St Mary's in June as planned

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028, because it would hit right as Grace and I start our life together, with no savings. What would help is paid apprenticeships for adults, and companies that train their own people instead of dropping them.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: You didn't ask about faith, and that matters to me. If things go wrong, the church and family will be there, not some app. I'd want people to remember that.

headlineQuote: If things go wrong, the church and family will be there, not some app.
portrait: David is a **27-year-old carvery cook** at an old market-town pub.
He's marrying Grace in June and has under **one month** saved.
He's **traditional**, wary of handouts and keen on trades and family.
He avoids **AI tools** and blames big brewery bosses for squeezes.
His mood rises to **alarmed** under fast AGI, mostly for his future family.
biggestWorry: He fears **AGI by 2028** most, hitting just as married life starts.
whatWouldHelp: He wants **paid adult apprenticeships** and employers who train their own staff.
